_readme: Client-side rate and concurrency limits per provider (W4-04). Held as data beside their sources rather than in code, so every limit's provenance is reviewable where the number lives. The file is bundled into @adaptic/utils at build time: changing a limit ships as a release of this package and a consumer bump, not as a runtime switch. Every entry states where its numbers came from: `published` means transcribed from that provider's documented ceiling with a source link, `conservative-default` means the ceiling is not yet known and the client is deliberately slower than it needs to be. A guessed high limit and a known high limit look identical in config and behave identically right up until the provider starts refusing requests, so they are never allowed to look the same here. `scope` states the unit the provider enforces its limits in: `model` keeps one independent guard per model, `provider` (the default) one guard for all of the provider's models; a `model` scope cites its source like any published number (`source` when the entry is published, `scope_source` otherwise). `requests_per_minute_basis` overrides `basis` for the per-minute number when a provider publishes one bound and not the other, so the unpublished number never borrows the published label. A provider whose scope is `model` may carry a `models` map of per-model overrides: each override replaces the provider's numbers for that one model only, states its own `basis`, and is held to the same provenance rules as a provider entry. It exists for a model whose role differs from its siblings' (the closed incumbent that absorbs a whole alias's traffic when every leg above it is out), not to loosen a provider wholesale. `requests_per_minute` is a REFILL RATE and not a bucket size. `max_burst` is the bucket size: the most requests the guard admits in one instant, which the refill rate does not determine. The two are separate because a single number bounds only the long-run average, and a bucket sized at its own refill period starts full - so the first instant of a cold process admits the whole period's allowance, which a provider enforcing its ceiling over a shorter window refuses however correct that average is. An entry that declares no `max_burst` keeps the per-minute allowance as its capacity, which is the behaviour the guard has always had; the field is therefore added without changing any entry that does not set it. It is deliberately UNSET for the providers above whose numbers were sized against measured starvation of the live decision path, because tightening their burst is a separate decision that needs its own measurement rather than a side effect of introducing the field - and refusing a call on that path lost decisions outright, so the conservative direction there is not the tight one. It is REQUIRED of any provider serving a decision route this package guards, enforced by the limits verifier, because such a route is admitted against a vendor whose ceiling is enforced per second and a route admitted without a declared capacity is admitted with its burst unbounded. `max_burst_basis` overrides `basis` for the capacity, on the same rule as `requests_per_minute_basis`: a capacity derived from the client's own refill rate is the client's choice even where the entry's other numbers were transcribed. A capacity is a MEASUREMENT and not a convention, so an entry that declares `max_burst` states where the number came from in three more fields. `max_burst_measured_demand` is the largest number of calls measured live demand can put on this guard in one instant, and the capacity must be at or above the lesser of it and `max_concurrent` - a call past the concurrency ceiling waits for a permit whatever the bucket holds, so the capacity's duty ends there. `max_burst_vendor_ceiling` is the vendor's own published bound on one instant, with `max_burst_vendor_ceiling_unit` naming the unit it was published in, and null where the vendor publishes no instantaneous bound at all; a per-minute allowance is never recorded here, because reading a minute's figure as a bound on an instant is the conflation this field exists to end. `max_burst_source` says where the demand figure and the ceiling figure each came from, including the read that would settle a null ceiling. And a capacity below this entry's own `max_concurrent` is refused unless its basis is published, because a bucket tighter than the concurrency ceiling paces calls that ceiling admits - and for an entry whose concurrency was sized against measured starvation of the live decision path, that is a throttle on that path arrived at by convention rather than measurement. A capacity set from a provider's refill rate for want of a figure is exactly that throttle: the right response to an unknown ceiling is the demand-derived capacity and a named read, never a tighter number nobody measured. One consequence is worth knowing wherever the capacity equals `max_concurrent`: the bucket, not the permits, is then what an instantaneous burst meets first, and the two queues do not end the same way. A caller waiting for a permit is bounded by its OWN budget, while a caller waiting for a token is bounded by `acquire_timeout_ms` alone, whatever budget it passed. So the over-capacity call is paced for up to that timeout rather than refused promptly into the fallback chain, which is the intended cost - latency, not decisions - only while the timeout leaves the caller enough of its deadline to still answer. An entry whose timeout does not is sized wrong in the timeout, not in the capacity.

defaults._readme: Applied to any provider whose published ceiling is unknown. Chosen to be comfortably below the slowest plausible published limit: being slower than necessary costs latency, while being faster than permitted costs 429s that the fallback chain will read as provider ill-health and use to open a circuit breaker. The asymmetry is what makes the conservative side the correct default.
defaults.max_burst_source: Derived from this block's own max_concurrent 12: the most calls that can be in flight in one instant, so the bucket never binds before the concurrency bound does. No vendor is named by a default block, so no instantaneous ceiling can be cited; demand is 0 because a provider with no entry has no route in either table and therefore no traffic.
defaults.note: Raised 2026-09-15 after the 4-concurrent ceiling was measured starving the live equity decision path: the alias chain reported 'exhausted its fallback chain' with every leg skipped by this guard (deepinfra primary+secondary and the anthropic incumbent), 173 of 473 signal-coordination calls failed (36.6%), and decisions were lost outright. Corroborating evidence at the time: ZERO 429s observed on any provider, the engine's own global fan-out gate permits 100 concurrent with 17 active, and 877 signal-analysis calls had been admitted to that gate. Concurrency and RPM are raised TOGETHER because they bind in series - lifting max_concurrent alone would only move the bottleneck to the token bucket. STILL conservative-default, NOT published: no provider console was read for these numbers, so they remain a deliberate under-estimate of an unknown ceiling. Transcribe the real tier limits (W3-07) and set basis to published.

anthropic.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 12, which is the most calls one instant can hold, so the capacity cannot pace a call the concurrency bound admits. VENDOR CEILING UNKNOWN: the scope_source publishes the UNIT (requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, per model class) and no per-second or concurrent-request bound, and the figure in force is the organisation's usage tier, read only from the Console. Read 2026-10-17. The same page documents the hazard this capacity exists for, in the vendor's own words: 'a rate of 60 requests per minute (RPM) might be enforced as 1 request per second', and 'The API uses the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting.' DEMAND 0: this provider-scoped guard covers claude-sonnet-5-5, the closed incumbent of llm.reason and llm.agentic, which is reached only when both DeepInfra legs of those aliases fail; no fallback was recorded in the measured window. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot. A reachable Anthropic figure that would replace the null ceiling is the anthropic-ratelimit-requests-limit response header on a live call from the engine, whose key is provisioned.
anthropic.note: The unit is per model: the scope_source states 'Rate limits are applied separately for each model; therefore you can use different models up to their respective limits simultaneously', measured as requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute for each model class, with no concurrency ceiling. Each model therefore gets its own guard, so traffic on one model class (an Opus incumbent serving background aliases) cannot refuse calls to another (the Haiku incumbent of the hot-path alias). The NUMBERS stay conservative-default: the organisation's usage tier sets the real ceilings and is read only from the Claude Console rate-limits page, which has not been transcribed. The lowest standard tier listed at the source allows 1,000 requests per minute per model; organisations with limited history can start on an evaluation tier below that, which is why these values are held well under it. Transcribe the tier's limits (W3-07) and set basis to published.

claude-haiku-4-5.max_burst_source: Derived from this override's own max_concurrent 48, which the note above sized by Little's law against the measured diversion of llm.fast's whole load onto this model. DEMAND 100 is that diverted cohort at its structural ceiling (the engine admits at most 100 concurrent monitoring sessions and reserves no live slot from a p0_trading call), and the capacity covers every one of them the concurrency gate can hold at once, which is 48: a call beyond that waits for a permit whatever the bucket holds, so a capacity above 48 would bound nothing this guard can reach. VENDOR CEILING UNKNOWN on the same reading as the provider entry: the unit is per model per minute and the figure is the organisation's tier. The capacity is stated here rather than inherited because an override replaces the provider's numbers for this model wholesale, and a capacity sized for 12 permits would refuse the traffic this model exists to absorb.
claude-haiku-4-5.note: Raised 2026-09-28 for the closed-incumbent role this model holds on llm.fast, llm.decide and llm.extract. Measured that day: when DeepInfra was capacity-limited ('Model busy, retry later', timeouts at the 30000 ms hot-path budget), both DeepInfra legs of llm.fast opened their breakers and ALL of the alias's traffic fell to this model, where the 12-permit guard could not absorb it. In the 12 minutes to 15:33Z the incumbent leg recorded 18 timeouts, 15 breaker-open and 11 guard refusals ('did not admit the call within 15000 ms'), and the chain exhausted 20-45 times per 5 minutes. Sizing: in-flight demand is arrival rate times leg duration (Little's law), and the leg duration that matters is the worst case the chain permits, 30 s. 12 permits at 30 s serve 24 calls/min; 48 permits serve 96 calls/min at 30 s and up to the 300/min rate bound at haiku's normal single-digit-second latency, which covers the diverted llm.fast load plus normal llm.decide/llm.extract volume on the same guard. requests_per_minute is raised with it (the two bind in series) to 300, which is 30% of the 1,000 requests per minute per model that the scope_source lists for the lowest standard tier, so it remains below any standard tier's ceiling; no Anthropic 429 was observed in the window. acquire_timeout_ms is cut from 15000 to 10000 so an admitted call keeps at least 20 s of its 30 s leg budget: a call admitted after a 15 s wait had half its budget left, timed out at the provider, and that timeout was charged to this route's breaker, which then refused every call for the cooldown. STILL conservative-default: the organisation's tier has not been transcribed from the Claude Console (W3-07). Other Anthropic models keep the provider numbers.

deepseek.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 12, the most calls one instant can hold. NO CEILING IS CITED, and not because none is published: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/rate_limit publishes a CONCURRENCY ceiling PER MODEL (deepseek-flash 2,500, deepseek-v4-pro 500 concurrent, a request counting as one connection until its response completes) and no per-minute or per-second bound. Read 2026-10-17. A per-model figure is not a bound on this guard, because this entry's scope is the provider and one guard holds every model it might reach; citing it here would read a figure across a unit it was not published in, which is the same conflation the capacity field exists to end. Setting scope to model against that source is what would let the figure be cited. DEMAND 0: no alias route names this provider and no DeepSeek key is provisioned on the engine service, so this guard is unreachable. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot.

deepinfra.max_burst_source: The one entry of the eight whose capacity had to be measured rather than derived, because this guard is the one a cold start can saturate. CEILING 200, published and per model, which is the unit this entry's scope already keeps: the source states 'Every account has a default limit of 200 concurrent requests per model' and 'The rate limit is on concurrent requests, not per-minute volume.' Read 2026-10-17. DeepInfra therefore publishes NO instantaneous request-RATE ceiling at all; the RPM-versus-duration table on that page is an explicitly derived illustration of the concurrency bound and is not carried as one. DEMAND 100, the most signal_analysis calls one instant can put on this guard, read from the engine's own bounds: maxConcurrentSessions 100 (engine src/config/equities/market-hours-config.ts) refuses the 101st symbol a monitoring session outright; signal_analysis is a p0_trading call kind, whose ceiling is the whole live pool, LLM_ADMISSION_LIVE_CONCURRENCY 100 with LLM_ADMISSION_P0_RESERVED 0; and llm.fast's primary leg is one model, so all 100 land on one guard. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot. Observed demand through this guard is far below that today - one call per five minutes, the llm.alias_probe heartbeat at 21/21 primary-leg answers - because the governed row llmAliasRouting reads mode legacy at rolloutPct 0, which serves every per-symbol decision through the consumer's direct transport and never through these guards. The 100 is therefore LATENT and the capacity is sized for it anyway: it arrives the instant that row is flipped, with no code change and no deploy, and the row exists to be flipped. Capacity 200 sits above that demand and at the only instantaneous ceiling the vendor publishes, so it bounds the burst without being the bound that paces a cold cohort: 100 is admitted in one instant with no wait, which is byte-identical to the conflated 240 on every burst these bounds can produce. The capacity a refill-rate convention would have given - 240/60 = 4 - would admit 4 + 4*15 = 64 of that cohort within acquire_timeout_ms and REFUSE the remaining 36 as a RateGuardTimeoutError, losing decisions on the live trading path to bound a burst the vendor does not measure. max_burst_basis stays conservative-default while the only published figure is in a different unit: a capacity read across from a concurrency ceiling is a client's choice anchored on the vendor's, not a transcription of it.
deepinfra.note: Transcribed 2026-09-23 from the source, which states 'Every account has a default limit of 200 concurrent requests per model', that two models queried simultaneously allow 400 in total (200 per model), and that 'The rate limit is on concurrent requests, not per-minute volume.' Concurrency is therefore the bound DeepInfra enforces, and it is enforced per MODEL, so each model gets its own guard at 200. One guard shared by the whole account enforced a ceiling DeepInfra does not impose, and because an alias's primary and secondary are both served from this account, it refused the secondary exactly when the primary's queue was full. DeepInfra publishes no per-minute ceiling, so requests_per_minute is the client's own pacing backstop (requests_per_minute_basis: conservative-default), keyed per model like the bound DeepInfra does enforce. Exceeding the ceiling returns HTTP 429, and a very busy model can return 429 below it. The ceiling belongs to the account and this guard to one process, so every process calling the same model through the same account shares the 200.

fireworks.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 12, the most calls one instant can hold. NO CEILING IS CITED because the published figure is not an instantaneous one: https://docs.fireworks.ai/guides/quotas_usage/rate-limits publishes 10 RPM without a payment method and 6,000 RPM with one, per MINUTE and account-wide, with no per-second and no concurrent-request bound. Read 2026-10-17. A per-minute figure is exactly what this field exists not to be read as a bound on an instant. DEMAND 0: no alias route names this provider, no Fireworks key is provisioned on the engine service, and the consumer's own provider list does not carry it, so neither path can reach this guard. zai.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 12, the most calls one instant can hold, and demand-derived pending a vendor figure. VENDOR CEILING UNKNOWN AND UNREAD: the vendor's documentation returned HTTP 404 at both https://docs.z.ai/guides/overview/rate-limits and https://docs.z.ai/guides/rate-limits, so there is no first-party page to transcribe in any unit. Read 2026-10-17. Third-party reports that Z.ai bounds concurrency and shows the figure only in its console are not carried as published. DEMAND 0, and no read is available to raise it: no alias route names this provider and no Z.ai key is provisioned on the engine service, so there is not even a 429 or a response header to measure from. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot. The GLM-5.3 leg of llm.reason is served BY DeepInfra under the model id zai-org/GLM-5.3 and is held by the deepinfra guard, so the name in that model id is not a path to this entry. The read that would settle the ceiling is the organisation's own console page, which needs an interactive login.

groq.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 2, which is already the tightest bound on this guard's instant, so the capacity changes nothing a call can reach. VENDOR CEILING UNKNOWN in any unit: https://console.groq.com/docs/rate-limits enumerates RPM, RPD, TPM, TPD, ASH, ASD, ITPM and OTPM, among which there is no per-second and no concurrent-request unit at all, and refers the figures to the account settings page. Read 2026-10-17. DEMAND 0: this entry's note records it as the declared primary of llm.fast blocked on open item OI-01, and the alias table now gives that alias a DeepInfra primary, so the declaration is stale and no route reaches this guard; no Groq key is provisioned on the engine service either. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot. Neither bound here could serve a cold cohort - at max_concurrent 2 the concurrency gate refuses one long before the bucket does - so sizing this entry for one is a measurement owed by whoever opens the route, not a number to invent now.
groq.note: Declared primary of the hot-path llm.fast alias but blocked on open item OI-01. Held tighter than the default because a hot-path caller cannot afford to queue: if the limit binds, failing fast into the chain beats waiting.

openrouter.max_burst_source: Derived from this entry's own max_concurrent 2, which is already the tightest bound on this guard's instant. VENDOR CEILING STRUCTURALLY UNKNOWABLE from the client, not merely unread: https://openrouter.ai/docs/api-reference/limits publishes 20 RPM only for model ids ending ':free', and states that a 429 'can come from two places: OpenRouter, when you hit one of the platform limits above... [or] the upstream provider, when the provider serving your request is rate limiting'. Read 2026-10-17. The instantaneous ceiling on a paid request is therefore whichever upstream the aggregator selects for it, which the client cannot observe, which is the same reason this entry's note already holds it tight. DEMAND 0: no alias route reaches it and no OpenRouter key is provisioned on the engine service. Demand read 2026-10-16 from the engine's own bounds and its live status snapshot.
openrouter.note: Aggregator backstop, reached by explicit route only. Held tight because its own limits are a function of whichever upstream it selects, which the client cannot observe.

typesafe.max_burst_source: One second of this entry's own refill, which is the tightest bound derivable where the vendor publishes the unit and no figure: a client cannot exceed, in any instant, a rate it already sustains. VENDOR CEILING UNKNOWN - the source page states the unit (tokens per second and requests per second) and refers both figures to a per-organisation console, and the API returns no rate-limit header to read one from. DEMAND 0: the typed routes have no caller that dispatches them, so no measured demand bounds this capacity from below and the capacity may stay at the unit's own floor. Raising it is a measurement: read the organisation's requests per second from the developer console, set source, and raise capacity no higher than that figure minus one second's refill.
typesafe.note: Provider of the typed decision routes dm.hosted and dm.hosted.preview, both of which the route table admits, so these numbers bind every call either route makes and are to be narrowed by measurement rather than left as defaults. THE VENDOR PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md section 'Rate limits' states, in full: 'Rate limits are set per organization. Your organization's current limits are in the developer console.' and 'Limits are measured in tokens per second and requests per second. A request over either limit returns 429 Too Many Requests.' Re-read 2026-10-17: the page carries no figure for either bound, the API returns no rate-limit response header to read one from, and the console that holds the organisation's own limits is reachable only by an interactive login. An earlier revision of this entry cited '100K tokens per second and 40 requests per second' and 'can change without notice' to this same page; neither string nor either figure is present at that source, so the citation is not verifiable and the figures are not carried. What IS documented, and all that this entry rests on, is the UNIT: the vendor enforces per SECOND. requests_per_minute 600 is the client's own pacing choice, 10 requests per second. max_burst 10 holds the bucket to one second of that refill, which is the tightest bound derivable without a vendor figure: a client that cannot read the ceiling can still guarantee it never offers more in any instant than the sustained pace it has already chosen, so no burst of its own making is what crosses a ceiling it cannot see. Conflating the two quantities is what made this unsafe - at a bucket sized to the per-minute allowance a cold process admitted 600 calls in one instant, sixty seconds of pacing spent before the first second elapsed, and a per-second ceiling refuses that however correct the minute's average is. max_burst_basis is conservative-default and stays there while source is null: a capacity whose vendor bound was never read is a choice, not a transcription. Raising it is a measurement, not a preference - read the organisation's requests per second from the developer console, set source, and raise capacity no higher than that figure minus one second's refill. No token-per-second bound is enforced here: this package does not count hosted tokens, so the vendor's other published unit is unguarded and a large-state request can cross it while every request bound holds. max_concurrent 8 is a second bound on the instant: at the latencies measured on these routes (281 to 313 ms for a one-question text call, 468 to 515 ms for a read over one 1024x768 image) eight in flight complete about 16 to 28 requests per second, so it binds above the capacity and the capacity is what holds the per-second rate. acquire_timeout_ms 250 is far below the 15000 default on purpose and must not exceed the route's budget_ms: the rate wait is bounded by this number alone, whatever budget the caller passes, and a typed step that has queued a quarter of a second cannot still answer inside a sub-second deadline, so it is refused as an admission fault and the caller moves on.
